questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{\sqrt{x}-2}{x-4} & =\frac{\sqrt{4}-2}{4-4}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{\sqrt{x}-2}{x-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-2)(\sqrt{x}+2)}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{x-4}{(x-4)(\sqrt{x}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {25}^{-}}\frac{2x-10\sqrt{x}}{x-25} & =\frac{50-10\sqrt{25}}{25-25}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {25}^{-}}\frac{2x-10\sqrt{x}}{x-25} & ={lim}_{x\to {25}^{-}}\frac{2(x-5\sqrt{x})}{x-25} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {25}^{-}}\frac{2(x-5\sqrt{x})(x+5\sqrt{x})}{(x-25)(x+5\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {25}^{-}}\frac{2({x}^{2}-{(5\sqrt{x})}^{2})}{(x-25)(x+5\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {25}^{-}}\frac{2({x}^{2}-25x)}{(x-25)(x+5\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {25}^{-}}\frac{2x(x-25)}{(x-25)(x+5\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {25}^{-}}\frac{2x}{x+5\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{2(25)}{25+5\sqrt{25}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=2$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{3x+1}-\sqrt{7}} & =\frac{2-2}{\sqrt{3(2)+1}-\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{2-2}{\sqrt{7}-\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{x-2}{\sqrt{3x+1}-\sqrt{7}} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{(\sqrt{3x+1}-\sqrt{7})(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{(\sqrt{3x+1})^{2}-(\sqrt{7})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{3x+1-7} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{3x-6} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(x-2)(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7})}{3(x-2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{7}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3(2)+1}+\sqrt{7}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{7}}{3} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{7}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{0+1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{x+1}-1)(\sqrt{x+1}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{x+1})^{2}-{1}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(x+1)-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\cancel{x}(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{\cancel{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\sqrt{x+1}+1) \\  & =\sqrt{0+1}+1 \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-9}{\sqrt{x+1}-2} & =\frac{{3}^{2}-9}{\sqrt{3+1}-2}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-9}{\sqrt{x+1}-2} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{({x}^{2}-9)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)}{(\sqrt{x+1}-2)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)}{(\sqrt{x+1})^{2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)}{(x+1)-4} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x-3)(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)}{x-3} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\cancel{(x-3)}(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)}{\cancel{x-3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\,(x+3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2) \\  & =(3+3)(\sqrt{3+1}+2) \\  & =6(4) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$
